blocks.text: This research plan proposes a formal theorem to address identified gaps in the survey regarding black hole formation mechanisms. The core hypothesis posits that in spherically symmetric stellar collapse, replacing pointwise energy conditions with the Averaged Null Energy Condition (AANEC) plus an explicit averaged null-convergence/focusing condition allows for the derivation of a trapped-surface threshold linked to Misner-Sharp compactness. This work aims to provide a rigorous formal proof that excludes stable non-black-hole remnants above a specific compactness-dependent mass scale within this restricted model class. However, significant research gaps remain concerning the specific mathematical formulation of the averaging condition and the identification of boundary variables in stellar evolution pathways. The plan treats the observed stellar mass gap as an astrophysical consistency constraint rather than a direct consequence of the formal theorem, acknowledging that explosion energetics and fallback processes introduce substantial uncertainty. Expected outcomes are conditional: the theorem will either support the proposed mechanism within the defined validity domain, yield partial or heterogeneous results requiring refinement, or be contradicted, in which case alternative explanations such as rotation or magnetic dynamics will be prioritized.

claim_provenance.statement: Identified gaps include the absence of a formal claim definition for AANEC in singularity theorems (SH3), the failure to map boundary variables in remnant formation pathways (SH4), and unresolved uncertainties in progenitor explosion energetics.

The proposed contribution is a formal theorem/conjecture establishing that AANEC plus an explicit averaged null-convergence/focusing condition forces trapped-surface formation at a model-dependent compactness threshold, thereby bounding stable non-black-hole remnants.

The prespecified analysis will evaluate whether the derived compactness bound is consistent with the declared relation under controlled assumptions, distinguishing valid theorem construction from null or contradictory outcomes.
